catalog_quote: El iñapari es un idioma tonal restringido. Es decir, en esta lengua el tono de la voz juega un papel limitado en la función comunicativa. Raras veces sirve para distinguir ítems léxicos como en el ticuna, ni tampoco funciona en el sistema gramatical como en el bora. Más bien, tiene el efecto culminativo de delimitar las palabras dentro de la cadena hablada. Entre los sustantivos y los adjetivos, cada palabra normalmente tiene un solo tono alto, aunque algunas palabras tienen dos. new_statements.quote: El iñapari es un idioma tonal restringido. [...] Entre los sustantivos y los adjetivos, cada palabra normalmente tiene un solo tono alto, aunque algunas palabras tienen dos. Salvo en el caso de algunas palabras bi-silábicas, el tono alto no suele caer en la primera sílaba de la palabra; esta sílaba, al igual que todas las sílabas que le siguen al tono alto, llevan un tono bajo. Así que lo más correcto sería clasificar el iñapari como una lengua de tono-acento (pitch-accent), igual que el nomatsiguenga. Aunque la ubicación del acento o tono alto en determinadas palabras es mayormente impredecible, hemos encontrado muy pocos casos de pares mínimos distinguidos solamente por el tono o acento.
new_statements.translation: Iñapari is a restricted tone language. [...] Among nouns and adjectives, each word normally has a single high tone, although some words have two. Except in the case of some disyllabic words, the high tone does not usually fall on the first syllable of the word; that syllable, like all the syllables that follow the high tone, bears low tone. So the most correct thing would be to classify Iñapari as a pitch-accent language, like Nomatsiguenga. Although the location of the accent or high tone in particular words is mostly unpredictable, we have found very few minimal pairs distinguished solely by tone or accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Culminative pitch accent: each (nominal/adjectival) word carries one high-toned syllable (occasionally two), whose position is lexically specified and 'mostly unpredictable'; it rarely falls on the word-initial syllable except in some disyllables, and every syllable after the H is low. Accent is marked with an acute on every entry in the vocabulary. Minimal pairs exist but are rare (anáwa 'they' vs anawá 'canoe').
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; some words carry two high tones (e.g. [iwáná] 'río', [aáwíri] 'flor'), and the two moras of a long vowel may differ in tone ([mapaá] 'colmena').
new_statements.exceptions: Some disyllables have H on the first syllable; a few words have two H tones; §4.1 sandhi: (i) the final low tone of many verb forms surfaces as high when another word follows within the phonological phrase (unless the next word begins with H); (ii) an underlying H on the second syllable of a disyllabic word is delinked when the preceding word ends in H (never applies to H on a first syllable or to words of three or more syllables).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (culminative, 'delimits words in the speech chain'); statement made for nouns and adjectives in citation form, with verbs discussed via phrase-level tone sandhi. Author frames the system as restricted tone / pitch accent rather than stress. Data from the last fluent speakers (one family, río Piedras, Madre de Dios, fieldwork 1993-94).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Iñapari (inap1242, ISO inp) as spoken by the last family of speakers on the río Piedras, Madre de Dios, Peru (Parker fieldwork 1993-94); no dialect distinction. SAPhon spells the page 'Inyapari'.

'La fonología y la ortografía', §4 'El tono' (pp. 17-24): Iñapari is a 'restricted tone language', best classified as pitch-accent like Nomatsiguenga; nouns/adjectives normally carry a single high tone (some two), culminative/delimitative; the high tone rarely falls on the first syllable except in some disyllables, all syllables after the H are low; the location of the accent/high tone is 'mayormente impredecible' (mostly unpredictable); very few minimal pairs ([anáwa] 'ellos' vs [anawá] 'canoa'); all high tones written with an acute in the vocabulary; §4.1 describes two sandhi processes…
